As a dedicated special education teacher, my role extends far beyond the classroom. I oversee the education and well-being of some of our most vulnerable students, many of whom present significant behavioral challenges that frequently result in physical altercations. Managing these behaviors requires not only patience and skill but also an immense amount of emotional and physical energy, as well as additional trainings. In addition to direct instruction, I am responsible for overseeing and supporting three educational technicians, ensuring that they have the guidance and resources necessary to effectively assist our students. While collaboration is essential, breaks throughout the day are scarce, leaving little time to reset and prepare for the next challenge. The demand of my workload far exceeds the compensation provided, making it difficult to sustain the level of dedication and commitment required in this field. Beyond classroom instruction and behavioral management, my responsibilities include writing Individualized Education Programs (IEPs), drafting Written Notices, and preparing other legally binding documents to ensure compliance with state and federal regulations. These documents require precision and extensive knowledge of each student's unique needs. Additionally, I regularly collaborate with other professionals, including speech and occupational therapists, behavior specialists, and administrators, to ensure that our students receive the most appropriate and effective education possible. Despite the extensive responsibilities, the financial compensation does not align with the time, effort, and expertise required to fulfill these duties effectively. Special education teachers play a critical role in shaping the futures of students who require individualized instruction and support, yet the current pay structure does not reflect the level of dedication and sacrifice required for this role. Our students deserve the best, and that starts with ensuring that their educators are valued and supported. Thank you for your time and consideration. I am writing today to express my full support for increasing the minimum salary for teachers in Maine.
Teachers are the backbone of our society, shaping the minds and futures of young people who will one day contribute to the workforce, our communities, and our state. They are tasked with more than just imparting academic knowledge--they serve as mentors, counselors, and role models for their students. They go above and beyond every day, often spending countless hours outside of the classroom, preparing lesson plans, grading assignments, attending professional development, and investing in the success of their students.
We must ensure that those who dedicate their lives to educating the next generation are compensated in a way that reflects their commitment, expertise, and the challenges they face in the classroom.
However, despite the immense responsibility placed on teachers, the base pay in Maine has not kept pace with the rising cost of living or the ever-growing demands of the profession. Many teachers in Maine struggle to make ends meet, and the gap between the salaries of educators and the cost of living is widening. This puts an undue burden on teachers and makes it harder for the state to attract and retain top talent in the profession. The result is a shortage of qualified teachers, especially in rural areas and certain specialized fields, which ultimately affects the quality of education for our children.
Increasing the base pay for teachers in Maine is not just a matter of fairness--it is an investment in the future of our state. Higher pay will help attract and retain the best educators, reduce turnover, and ensure that our students receive a high-quality education. Teachers who feel valued and supported are more likely to remain in the profession, dedicate themselves to their students, and contribute to the broader community.
Furthermore, when we invest in education, we invest in the future success of Maine's economy. High-quality education leads to a more skilled and knowledgeable workforce, which is essential for attracting businesses and fostering innovation. Supporting our teachers is one of the most effective ways we can ensure Maine's long-term prosperity.
In conclusion, I urge you to prioritize increasing the minimum salary for teachers in Maine. By doing so, we send a clear message that we value the hard work and dedication of our educators and are committed to providing them with the compensation they deserve. Our teachers are essential to our state's future, and it is time that we recognize and reward their contributions accordingly.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Ashley Cirone Harrington Elementary School 2024 Washington County Teacher of the Year

Testimony in Support of LD 34 An Act to Increase the Minimum Salary for Teachers
Senator Rafferty, Representative Brennan, and Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee,
I am submitting testimony in support of LD 34. While I approach this bill with some hesitation, I believe it addresses a very real problem that Maine can no longer ignore.
Maine has one of the highest per-pupil spending rates in the country, yet student outcomes continue to decline. That reality should concern every taxpayer and every policymaker in this state. Simply spending more money without structural accountability will not solve the problem.
However, one issue that is undeniably contributing to the decline in our education system is the growing crisis in teacher recruitment and retention.
Across Maine, schools are struggling to fill positions. Many districts are relying on long-term substitutes or emergency certifications. Young people who might otherwise consider teaching are choosing different careers because the compensation does not justify the level of education, responsibility, and workload required.
LD 34 takes a modest step toward addressing that problem by gradually increasing the minimum teacher salary from $40,000 to $45,000 in 2026-2027, then to $47,500 in 2027-2028, and finally to $50,000 in 2028-2029
That increase will not solve all of Maine's workforce challenges in education, but it moves the conversation in the right direction. If we expect qualified professionals to enter and remain in the classroom, the starting salary must at least be competitive with other professions requiring similar education levels.
At the same time, I want to be clear that increasing minimum salaries cannot be the only policy response. Maine must also begin having serious conversations about:
� how education dollars are being spent � how administrative costs are growing � how we measure educational outcomes and student achievement
Taxpayers deserve to know that increased investment in salaries is paired with responsible oversight and a renewed focus on student success.
In short, if we want strong schools, we must attract and retain strong teachers. Right now Maine is struggling to do that.
For those reasons, I support LD 34 as a reasonable step forward while encouraging the Legislature to continue addressing the broader structural issues affecting education in this state.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Colleen Brown

Please let the text below serve as my testimony in support of L.D. 34: "An Act to Increase the Minimum Salary for Teachers," scheduled for hearing on February 26th, 2025.
At a basic level, the combination of formal education, internship, and licensing exam that is necessary to become a teacher makes the occupation part of the professional class. The education and training that teachers undertake is pivotal to maintaining teacher quality, but there is an economic divide right at the outset. In many cases, prospective teachers assume significant student debt to pay for their education and training, which makes their financial situation and long-term place in the field more tenuous than peers who come from wealthier households, placing those less wealthy teachers at a significant disadvantage. And what is more, the continuing education and professional development expectations likewise require significant time, effort, and money that may not be subsidized by the employing district in part or at all, depending on the employment contract. All of this makes compensation a prominent barrier to teachers entering and staying in the classroom at every level and in every discipline.
If teaching is in fact a professional job with demands comparable other fields, then its average compensation package, including salary, must be competitive with other comparable fields in order to address those economic realities. According to a 2022 NEA poll, 78% of teachers surveyed said that low pay is a "serious" issue in the profession, with 48% of that total stating that low pay is a "very serious" issue. That same poll indicated that 96% of those surveyed said that raising teacher salaries would be important to addressing teacher burnout. A related 2023 survey by the Economic Policy Institute that was based on United States Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed that the teacher compensation penalty relative to other professions in 2023 was 26.6%, or 73.4 cents on the dollar. That penalty is a disparity that has lifechanging implications, potentially dictating whether teachers are able to pay down their student debt, buy homes in the communities they serve, or prepare for a stable and dignified retirement.

L.D. 34 seeks to close that early-career pay gap and address many of those issues. The bill's initial adjustments between 2026 and 2030 that will be subsidized by state monies are critical to recruiting the next generation of teachers and helping districts big and small adjust their budgeting practices toward being sustainable. Then, the bill's cost-of-living adjustments made annually in 2030 and thereafter are essential to keeping pay competitive and keeping district budgets aligned with predictable salary costs year-over-year. The two-pronged approach to L.D. 34 is prudent in the short-term and long-term, and the bill's bipartisan sponsorship illustrates that the legislators of Maine know that this is an urgent and important step in a positive direction.
Moreover, L.D. 34 should help to remedy disparities between early-career compensation in different districts and regions. Pre-service and novice teachers would have greater flexibility in seeking out positions that suit their talents regardless of whether the district is rural or urban, small or large. Veteran teachers would feel less pressure to move southward in search of greater lifetime earnings because they would already have an equitable financial foundation. Teachers from out-of-state would be better able to justify relocating to Maine and capitalizing on our outstanding local control districts, curricular freedom, committed colleagues, and community-oriented families and students if they can expect compensation that is competitive to their home state. All of these changes would help fill teaching positions with the best possible candidates from the widest variety of qualified applicant pools.
Education is an essential public service, and teachers are an important pillar in that service. We must do whatever we can to recruit and retain teachers. The Maine Department of Education's #TeachMaine framework emphasizes that fact; the State of Maine's Economic Development Strategy depends on that fact. Every child in every classroom deserves a qualified teacher, and L.D. 34 presents one important step in support of that goal.
I urge you to vote in favor of L.D. 34 and thank you for your time.
Sincerely,

Valerie Caruso I have worked in public education for 35 years.
Teachers are the backbone of our education system. They shape the minds of future generations, instill values, and inspire students to reach their full potential. Despite the immense impact they have on society, many teachers are not compensated fairly for their hard work and dedication. It is my firm belief that the minimum salary for teachers should be increased. Doing so would not only acknowledge the value of their contributions but also help attract and retain the best talent, ultimately improving the quality of education for students everywhere.
The Underappreciation of Teachers
Teachers are often undervalued in society, and their salaries are a reflection of this. According to various reports, teachers in many parts of the world are paid far less than professionals with comparable education and experience in other fields. In the United States, for instance, the average salary for teachers is lower than that of many other professions requiring similar levels of education. In many cases, teachers must supplement their income by taking on second jobs or spending their own money on classroom supplies. This financial strain can be disheartening for those who are already dedicating their time and energy to shaping the minds of young people. Increasing the minimum salary for teachers would not only provide them with a fair wage but would also send a message that society truly values the important role they play.
The Importance of Competitive Salaries in Attracting Talent
One of the most significant reasons for raising teachers' salaries is to attract talented individuals to the profession. A higher salary is often a key factor in career decisions. Right now, many bright, capable individuals are deterred from entering the teaching field due to its relatively low pay. In professions such as engineering, technology, or medicine, individuals with similar levels of education often earn significantly higher salaries. This creates a competitive disadvantage for teaching, despite the fact that it requires a deep commitment to both intellectual and emotional labor. By increasing the minimum salary for teachers, we can make the profession more appealing to talented individuals and ensure that the best candidates are choosing to become educators.
The Impact on Teacher Retention and Morale
Teacher retention is a growing concern, with many educators leaving the profession within a few years due to burnout, lack of support, and, critically, insufficient compensation. Increasing the minimum salary for teachers would play a vital role in retaining experienced educators. Teachers who feel adequately compensated are more likely to stay in the profession, which benefits both the students they teach and the education system as a whole. A higher salary also helps improve teacher morale. When teachers feel valued and financially secure, they are better able to focus on what really matters: providing quality education to their students. This, in turn, creates a positive learning environment and enhances student outcomes.
The Societal Benefits of Investing in Teachers
Increasing teachers' salaries is not just an investment in individual educators; it is an investment in society as a whole. Teachers play a critical role in shaping the future workforce and fostering a knowledgeable, skilled, and compassionate society. When teachers are compensated fairly, they are able to focus on their work without the constant stress of financial instability. This leads to better educational outcomes, which ultimately benefits everyone. Strong, well-funded education systems contribute to lower crime rates, higher levels of civic engagement, and a more productive economy. By increasing the minimum salary for teachers, we are ensuring that the foundation of our society--our education system--remains strong and effective.

Conclusion
In conclusion, increasing the minimum salary for teachers is a necessary step toward ensuring that our education system thrives. Teachers deserve to be paid fairly for the hard work, dedication, and impact they have on society. By offering higher salaries, we can attract talented individuals to the profession, retain experienced educators, and improve overall educational quality. Moreover, this investment in teachers will have long-term societal benefits, helping to build a stronger, more prosperous future for everyone. It is time for us to prioritize education and give teachers the compensation they truly deserve.
